Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The ocean town struggles to provide basic public services as more men gather at the railroad station seeking scarce work.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The narrator reflects on economic decline, racialized competition for scarce work, and fading hopes of prosperity through observations of unemployed laborers, Santos’s dream of retiring in Guatemala, and memories of an ambitious father. The meditation concludes that happiness lies not in wealth or retirement but in fleeting moments of relief and self-awareness, exposing the emptiness beneath inequality and abandoned community life.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Every, Because, Hispanics

outputs.L1:
My ocean town struggles to collect leaves, offer summer school, and keep our library open. Each day, more men stand at the railroad station, waiting to be chosen for work. Because Hispanics are thought to work for less, they are picked first, while the white and Black men avoid the terror in one another’s eyes.

Our handyman, Santos, who expects only what his hands earn, is proud of his half-acre in Guatemala, where he plans to retire. His desire to proceed with dignity is admirable, but he knows that now no one retires; everyone simply works harder.

My father imagined a life more satisfying than the one he managed to lead. He did not see himself as uneducated, thwarted, or bitter, but as soon-to-be rich. Being rich was his right, he believed. Happiness, I used to think, was a necessary illusion. Now I think it is merely a collection of precious moments of relief, like dreams of Guatemala.

Sometimes, on winter nights, surrounded by the profound silence of empty mansions—once cottages where people lived their lives, now owned by banks and the absent rich—I like to stand at my window, searching for the futile flicker of a television. Instead, I am always surprised to see the quaint, porous face of my reflection, immersed in its one abundance.
outputs.L2:
My seaside community cannot manage to clear fallen leaves, run classes during the summer, or prevent the library from closing. These days, increasing numbers of men gather daily at the train station, hoping someone will hire them. Hispanics are selected first because employers assume they will accept lower wages; meanwhile, the white and Black workers try not to recognize the fear reflected in each other’s faces.

Santos, our handyman, asks for nothing beyond what his labor earns. He takes pride in the half-acre of land he owns in Guatemala, where he hopes eventually to settle in retirement. His determination to move through life with dignity deserves respect, though he understands that retirement is no longer possible: everyone simply works more.

My father pictured a future far more fulfilling than the life he ultimately had. Rather than considering himself poorly educated, defeated, or resentful, he regarded himself as a man on the verge of wealth. He believed prosperity was something he deserved. I once saw happiness as an illusion people needed in order to live. Now, I understand it as a handful of treasured pauses from hardship—visions of Guatemala, for example.

On winter nights, I sometimes stand at my window amid the meaningful quiet of vacant mansions. Those buildings were once modest cottages filled with ordinary lives; today, they belong to banks and wealthy owners who are rarely present. I search for the pointless shimmer of a television screen, but instead I am always startled to find my own old-fashioned, permeable face in the glass, absorbed in the single form of abundance it possesses.
outputs.L3:
The ocean town is increasingly unable to provide even basic public services as growing numbers of unemployed men gather at the railroad station, hoping to secure whatever scarce work may be available. Competition for these jobs exposes the community’s racial and economic tensions. Hispanic laborers are often selected first because employers assume they will accept lower wages. Meanwhile, white and Black workers are linked by an unspoken recognition that, despite their differences, they share the same fear of poverty and economic desperation.

Among these workers is Santos, a proud and capable handyman who dreams of eventually returning to Guatemala and retiring on the half acre of land he owns there. Yet he understands that retirement has become an increasingly unrealistic hope. In the present economy, people cannot expect to rest after years of labor; instead, they must work longer and harder simply to survive.

The speaker places this reality in contrast with the worldview of the previous generation. The speaker’s father believed that wealth and success were his natural right, something he could confidently expect from life. The speaker, however, has developed a more modest and fragile understanding of happiness. Rather than seeing it as permanent security or prosperity, the speaker experiences happiness only in brief moments of relief from hardship.

This sense of decline is reflected in the town’s physical landscape. Large mansions stand empty under bank ownership, symbols of both former abundance and present failure. Together with the speaker’s reflections, these abandoned homes reveal a community profoundly reshaped by inequality, absence, and loss. What once appeared to promise comfort and prosperity now bears witness to displacement, economic insecurity, and the disappearance of an older way of life.
outputs.L4:
Every morning, men gathered near the hardware store before the sun had fully risen. They stood in small groups along the curb, carrying battered lunch pails and wearing work boots whitened by dust from jobs that no longer existed. Whenever a pickup slowed, they straightened and watched the driver, hoping to be chosen for a day of roofing, hauling, or demolition. Most trucks passed without stopping. By midmorning, the men drifted away one by one, their shoulders lowered beneath the weight of another wasted day.

Scarcity had made everyone suspicious. Workers who once shared food and tools now measured one another as rivals. Race and language became convenient explanations for suffering: one group was accused of accepting too little, another of demanding too much, and everyone believed someone else had stolen the future promised to them. The real causes—closed factories, vanished unions, neglected neighborhoods, and owners who had moved their money elsewhere—were harder to confront. It was easier to resent the man standing beside you than the distant system that had left you both waiting.

Santos spoke often of Guatemala. He imagined returning with enough savings to buy a small house and a patch of land where he could grow coffee, beans, and fruit. In his stories, the mornings were cool, the mountains green, and nobody hurried him. Retirement there would be a long, peaceful afternoon: a chair beneath a tree, grandchildren nearby, and no foreman calling his name.

Yet every year the dream receded. Rent increased. Relatives needed help. Work became less regular, and the money Santos managed to save disappeared during weeks when nobody hired him. Guatemala remained bright in his mind precisely because it was far away. It was not so much a destination as a promise that his years of labor had meaning.

Listening to him, I thought of my father. He had believed in advancement with an almost religious certainty. He worked overtime, studied advertisements for houses we could not afford, and spoke of promotions as though they were steps on a staircase built especially for him. He wanted more than comfort. He wanted proof that effort could transform a life.

For a while, his ambition seemed noble. Later, I understood how thoroughly it had consumed him. Each achievement produced another desire, and each disappointment felt like a judgment on his worth. He postponed rest, friendship, and pleasure because he believed happiness would begin after the next raise, the next purchase, or the next move. By the time he recognized that prosperity had no finish line, much of his life had already been spent running toward it.

Perhaps Santos’s retirement dream and my father’s hunger for success were versions of the same hope: the belief that happiness waited elsewhere. One looked backward toward a homeland made perfect by distance; the other looked forward toward a wealth that could never be sufficient. Both endured the present by imagining an escape from it.

But happiness, when it came at all, arrived without wealth or permission. It appeared in brief pauses: the moment a headache faded, the first cool breath after a day of heat, laughter among tired workers, or the sudden recognition that one was alive and aware. Such moments could not be stored, purchased, or postponed. They offered no security. They merely interrupted suffering long enough to reveal how much of life had been surrendered to fear and expectation.

Around us, the neighborhood continued to empty. Shops closed, porches sagged, and public spaces where people had once gathered became parking lots or fenced-off ruins. Inequality remained visible in every direction, yet it concealed a deeper emptiness shared by those with little and those who possessed too much. The poor were denied stability; the prosperous were taught never to feel satisfied.

There was no simple consolation in that knowledge. It did not restore the lost jobs or fulfill Santos’s dream. It did not return my father’s years. Still, recognizing the illusion brought a small kind of freedom. If happiness was not a reward waiting at the end of labor, then perhaps it could be found—briefly and imperfectly—in the act of seeing our lives clearly, before the moment passed.

This diversity deserves recognition because understanding different cultures encourages respect, inclusion, and unity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person prose poem about economic decline in a wealthy seaside town, immigrant day laborers, the illusion of prosperity, and finding brief moments of happiness amid inequality.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, the sea polished every window in town until even the empty houses looked inhabited. Light poured over the balconies, the marble foyers, the blue pools holding their breath behind locked gates. From the bluff, prosperity seemed permanent—a white sail stitched to the horizon, a promise no weather could undo.

But I knew the grocery store where three cashiers had vanished, the hotel that closed one wing and called it renovation, the bank notices folded discreetly beneath silver mail slots. I watched restaurants shorten their hours while keeping candles lit on every table. We were skilled at appearances. We parked our debts beneath flowering trees. We let the ocean speak loudly enough to cover the sound of everything breaking.

Each morning, immigrant men gathered beside the hardware store, lunch wrapped in foil, hands ready for whatever the town required: lifting stone, scraping paint, repairing roofs above rooms they would never enter as guests. Contractors slowed their trucks without stopping. Some days a few men climbed in. The others remained, telling jokes, sharing coffee, turning waiting into a country of its own.

I passed them with my small bag of oranges and felt the old shame of having enough, then not enough, then more than someone else. Wealth here was a tide chart written by strangers. It rose in certain gardens, withdrew from certain kitchens. It left boats gleaming in the harbor and families counting coins under fluorescent light.

Still, happiness came, disobedient and brief. A worker peeled an orange and handed half to his friend. Someone’s radio found a song bright enough to make three men dance beside the lumber racks. Gulls wheeled above us like scraps of torn paper. For one minute the sea belonged to no one, and the sun laid the same gold on every face.

I carried that minute home carefully.

By evening, the mansions shone along the cliffs, each one a lantern advertising a life without fear. Below them, the tide worried the seawall stone by stone. I stood at the water’s edge and listened—not for collapse, not for rescue, but for the small human music between them: laughter from the bus stop, a bottle rolling in the sand, two children racing the dark.

The town kept pretending to be rich. We kept finding ways to be alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective passage narrated by someone watching unemployed men gather at a railroad station, contrasting a Guatemalan handyman’s dream of retirement with the narrator’s father’s failed dream of becoming rich.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning the unemployed men gathered beneath the station clock, though none of them had trains to catch. They stood with paper cups warming their hands, watching commuters hurry toward offices, watching freight cars drag their burdens west. From a distance, they looked like passengers waiting for a country that had forgotten to arrive.

Among them was Tomás, a Guatemalan handyman who could mend anything except, he said, the years. He dreamed not of wealth but of stopping: a small cement house near Lake Atitlán, a garden with lime trees, a chair facing the volcanoes. Retirement, to him, meant waking without an alarm and owning the whole afternoon.

My father had dreamed in the opposite direction. He wanted money to carry him beyond restlessness—to make him important, envied, safe. Each failed business only sharpened the next promise. He died believing riches had missed him by inches.

Watching Tomás measure his future in shade and silence, I wondered whether my father had mistaken motion for arrival. The rails shone beside us, running toward places none of the men could afford to go. Above the platform, the clock kept perfect time, though for those waiting below it, time seemed less like a road than a room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a socially conscious prose poem that begins with a town cutting public services and ends with the speaker seeing their reflection in a dark window surrounded by empty mansions owned by banks and absentee elites.
counterfactuals.output:
The town began by cutting public services: first the late bus, then the library’s evening hours, then the clinic where mothers waited beneath a clock that had forgotten how to move. They called it balance, though no one asked what weight a child’s fever placed on the scale, or how far an old man could walk with groceries and a tired heart.

Soon the streetlights went dark on every third block. Potholes opened like mouths. Teachers bought pencils with wages already promised to rent, while the council unveiled a bright rendering of a future plaza, all glass and fountains, sponsored by men whose names appeared on buildings but never on ballots. We learned that scarcity has a careful geography: it settles where the poor live and lifts wherever money wants a view.

The mills had closed years ago, but their brick shells still held the weather. At dusk, workers crossed the river toward jobs that paid them just enough to return tomorrow. Notices bloomed on doors—FINAL, OVERDUE, VACATE—while luxury houses climbed the hill, each with twelve windows and no lamps lit. Their lawns were clipped by hands that could never afford the rooms behind them.

They told us the market was recovering. They told us to be resilient, as if resilience were not the name given to suffering when those in power have grown bored of hearing about it. The shelter filled. The school roof leaked. Somewhere, behind tinted glass, a ledger declared the town healthy.

I walked home past the shuttered fire station and the chained playground, past porches where neighbors shared soup beneath blankets, until I reached the hill and saw my reflection in a dark window, surrounded by empty mansions owned by banks and absentee elites.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic literary meditation on race, labor, class, and the American Dream, using images of leaf-strewn streets, closed libraries, day workers, abandoned cottages, and a flickering television.
counterfactuals.output:
By late October, the streets were covered in leaves the color of old pennies. They gathered in the gutters and along the curbs, where rain pressed them into dark, indistinguishable layers. In the wealthier neighborhoods, men arrived before dawn with blowers strapped to their backs, driving the leaves into bright heaps. By noon, the sidewalks were clean again, as though autumn itself had been politely removed.

The men rode home in the beds of trucks, knees touching, hands furred with dust. They passed the closed library on Jefferson Avenue, its stone steps scattered with maple leaves, its brass doors chained. Above them, carved into the lintel, were words about knowledge and freedom. The city had shuttered the building when the tax base failed, though no one could say exactly how a tax base failed, or why failure so often settled in the same ZIP codes.

Once, schoolchildren had waited there for their mothers to finish shifts at the hospital, the hotel, the poultry plant. Old men had read newspapers beneath green lamps. Job seekers had learned to type names and passwords into public computers. Now the windows reflected only traffic and sky. Knowledge remained inside, orderly on its shelves, while need stood outside in the weather.

Beyond the avenue, day workers waited in the parking lot of a hardware store. They waited with thermoses between their shoes and hoods pulled over their heads. Some were Black men whose fathers had come north for factory wages; some were brown men who had crossed deserts, rivers, checkpoints, and years. Each morning, pickup trucks slowed before them. A driver lowered his window and named a price. A few men climbed in. The others resumed waiting.

Work was said to confer dignity, though the dignity seemed to belong mainly to those who purchased it cheaply.

At the edge of town stood a row of abandoned cottages, built when the mill still made something the country believed it needed. Their porches sagged toward the weeds. Curtains, gray with mildew, hung in one window as if someone had stepped out only briefly. In another cottage, a child’s height marks remained penciled beside a kitchen door: six years, seven, eight. The roof had caved in above them. A young birch grew through the floorboards, pale and slender, reclaiming the room.

These houses had once been proof. A mortgage, a lawn, a secondhand car: small certificates of arrival. The American Dream was always spoken of as a road, but roads are built through certain neighborhoods and around others. Some families inherited maps. Some inherited tolls. Some were told to run faster while carrying the history of fields, kitchens, rail lines, laundries, mines.

At night, in the last occupied cottage, a television flickered blue against the walls. It showed a family in a spotless home buying things on credit. It showed candidates beneath flags, speaking of opportunity in voices trained not to tremble. It showed police lights, stock prices, smiling workers in hard hats. Between advertisements, the nation appeared briefly to itself and looked away.

An old woman watched from a chair beside the radiator. Her father had laid track; her mother had cleaned rooms she was never allowed to rent. She had spent thirty-two years sewing cuffs in a factory that moved south, then overseas, then nowhere anyone she knew could point to. On the mantel stood photographs of children who had left for better cities and found the same locked doors painted different colors.

Outside, the leaves moved along the empty street in restless companies. They scraped past the library, the parking lot, the cottages with their blind windows. They made a sound like distant applause, though there was no one to receive it.

The television flickered. The old woman slept. Somewhere before dawn, the day workers would rise and stand again beneath the cold white lamps, offering their bodies to the machinery of other people’s hopes. And the country, dreaming of itself as young and boundless, would wake without remembering who had labored through the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental, tightly formatted monologue about an ocean town in recession, a dignified worker named Santos who owns half an acre in Guatemala, and a narrator reconsidering whether happiness is an illusion or merely a moment of relief.
counterfactuals.output:
LOW TIDE, LOW WAGES

The ocean keeps arriving  
as if the town still matters.

Boarded arcade.  
Empty cannery.  
Three gulls fighting over a receipt.

We call it recession because collapse sounds deliberate.

Santos cleans the motel rooms with his collar buttoned. Dignity, in him, is not pride but precision: corners tucked, mirrors cleared, each soap centered in its little dish. He owns half an acre in Guatemala. Coffee plants. A zinc-roof house. Soil dark enough, he says, to remember rain.

I envy this proof of elsewhere.

At noon we sit behind the laundry, where the machines shake the wall like a distant engine. Santos eats an orange slowly. The sea flashes between warehouses. For one minute no manager calls, no bill opens its mouth, no future leans over us with a clipboard.

I used to think happiness was an illusion—

cheap light on deep water,  
a trick of distance,  
the town’s last advertisement.

Now I wonder if I asked too much of it.

Perhaps happiness is not a country, not ownership, not escape. Perhaps it is only relief with its shoes off. A clean room before the next guest. Half an acre waiting through the dry season. An orange divided into shining pieces.

The ocean withdraws.

The ocean returns.

Santos saves the seeds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
